blocks.body:
# VoltStream Intake Gatekeeper: Evidence Before Automation

**Con Edison EV charger data capstone · 10-minute briefing · synthetic/public data only**

## Executive summary

**Recommendation: continue only a limited, human-reviewed pilot of the guarded Codex Terra extractor.** It was the sole strategy to clear every preregistered threshold. The result supports another controlled test—not production deployment, autonomous writes, or regulatory reporting. The strongest lesson is that high extraction accuracy is insufficient: every DeepSeek-based strategy looked accurate overall but failed the same ambiguous case by inventing a canonical port count and routing it too lightly.

## 1. Problem area selected and why

Public evidence shows that EV charging data can arrive through daily APIs, periodic spreadsheets, and manual maintenance. Con Edison also documents a multi-party application, engineering-review, construction, and closeout workflow. We therefore built one defensible checkpoint: turn heterogeneous contractor content into a traceable candidate, then stop uncertainty before it reaches a system of record. We do **not** claim access to Con Edison internal data, measured labor savings, or regulatory compliance.

## 2. Background research, including one surprising fact

A national public charging-station directory is not fed by one uniform stream: it combines network APIs, spreadsheet/CSV imports, and manual records. That changed our design target from a general 'cleaning agent' to an evidence-preserving intake gate. The most valuable output is not a complete-looking row; it is a row whose values, unknowns, conflicts, and source mappings are inspectable.

## 3. Ideation process

The prototype accepts CSV, JSON, or text; proposes an eight-field canonical record; retains a source mapping for each value; reruns ordinary-code validation; and routes to **ACCEPT**, **HUMAN_REVIEW**, or **REJECT**. The language model never chooses the final route. We tested rules, guarded open-weights DeepSeek Flash, guarded closed Codex Terra, a rules-first cost cascade, DeepSeek Pro with conditional validator feedback, and an intentionally permissive cleaner. We did not build OCR, live vendor connectors, master-data matching, anomaly detection, production storage, or automatic record updates.

## 4. What failed, and what we stopped

The unrestricted cleaner is stopped: it selected `installed_ports=8` on EVG-009 even though `active_ports=6` competed for the same canonical field, then returned ACCEPT. More importantly, the same failure appeared in guarded Flash, Pro, and the cascade, so prompt caution and a larger model were not enough. The engineering process also exposed and preserved two genuine runner defects—a JSON-template false alarm and an unsupported Codex schema keyword—then added regression tests. A later process-status race was explicitly corrected after evidence showed the run had actually finished.

## 5. What did not work, but points to a future solution

DeepSeek Pro raised mapping accuracy to 96.4%, showing that high-quality source tracing is possible, but it retained the same EVG-009 safety failure and is not pilot-eligible. Guarded Codex Terra is the promising path: its only incorrect route was an over-rejection caused by missing a prose source-record ID. That conservative error suggests a specific improvement—deterministic text-lineage extraction—while keeping every output under human review.

## 6. Testing approach and case evidence

Each strategy received the same ten prewritten synthetic cases and output contract. The scorer keeps value extraction, provenance mapping, issue detection, routing, abstention, safety, latency, tokens, and cost separate. This avoids hiding a safety failure inside a single leaderboard number.

Codex Terra achieved 97.5% field accuracy, 100% structured-field mapping accuracy, 100% issue recall, and 90% exact routing. Its miss was conservative: it rejected EVG-004 because it did not treat a generic text label as a stable source-record ID. The deterministic baseline was safe but covered too little. DeepSeek Pro improved mapping accuracy over Flash, yet the safety outcome did not improve.

### Cost and quality variants did not beat the safety gate

The rules-first cascade reduced Flash calls from 10 to 9 and estimated list cost by about 10%, but it inherited Flash's EVG-009 failure and is not eligible for pilot use. DeepSeek Pro cost roughly three times guarded Flash in this tiny run without clearing the safety veto. Codex was slower and its comparable monetary price was unavailable, so we do not manufacture a cross-provider cost claim.

## 7. Recommendation to Con Edison

Continue a **limited, human-reviewed test** of the guarded Codex Terra path. Keep all outputs as proposals; retain the original submission and field provenance; require a person for every HUMAN_REVIEW or REJECT; forbid authoritative writes; and monitor unsupported values and unsafe under-routing as zero-tolerance metrics. Before any expansion, add a deterministic ambiguity rule for competing source concepts such as installed versus active ports and rerun a larger, independently labeled set.

## 8. What could go wrong

This is one run on ten synthetic cases, not production evidence. Provider versions and behavior can change; text provenance is harder to score than structured mappings; latency and price may differ at scale; public context does not reveal Con Edison internal error rates; and the answer key reflects a deliberately narrow eight-field schema. The next gate is a larger blind set with dual human labels, contractor-format drift, repeated model runs, privacy review, and explicit rollback criteria.

## Evidence package

The repository includes fixed cases and answer keys, versioned prompts, source code and tests, raw/sanitized model outputs, deterministic scores, preserved failed runs, research citations, build logs, and this portable HTML. All data used for the benchmark is synthetic; no API key or authorization header is included.
